evidence.quote: Consisting principally of carefully selected extracts from relevant scientific correspondence, with explanatory notes, the report emphatically (and quite correctly) asserts Newton’s priority, and heavily (and quite unjustly) implies plagiarism on Leibniz’s part.

findings.claim: Newton derived Kepler’s idealized planetary rules from inverse-square gravitation.

findings.claim: Keynes acquired many alchemical papers in and after 1936 and called Newton the last of the magicians.
findings.explanation: Independently authored scholarly accounts by Mandelbrote and Iliffe contextualize Keynes’s collection and interpretation. Iliffe explicitly distinguishes purchases at the sale and afterward; the exact short characterization is present in both accounts. These are scholarly analyses rather than two bare reproductions of the lecture.

evidence.quote: In 1936, the 'personal' papers that had been returned to the family were sold at auction in order to meet death duties and other family expenses.
evidence.origin: Scott Mandelbrote, Cambridge University Library Footprints of the Lion scholarly catalogue

evidence.quote: The economist, John Maynard Keynes, bought many of them and subsequently formed the view that Newton was 'the last of the magicians'.
evidence.origin: Scott Mandelbrote, Cambridge University Library Footprints of the Lion scholarly catalogue

evidence.quote: Keynes’s comments, based on the largely alchemical papers he had bought at the Sotheby Sale and later
evidence.origin: Rob Iliffe, Newton’s Religious Life and Work

evidence.quote: Keynes only collected in earnest after the sale had ended, and spent many months trying to add to his collection.
evidence.origin: Rob Iliffe, Newton’s Religious Life and Work

evidence.quote: Keynes’s Newton was not the first scientist but “the last of the magicians, the last of the Babylonians and Sumerians”

findings.claim: Voltaire printed an early version of the apple story in 1727.
findings.explanation: This verifies the existence and date of an explicitly attributed printed version of the legend, not the historical truth of a moment of discovery. Voltaire is one earlier transmitter alongside Stukeley.

evidence.quote: Voltaire then wrote in his Essay on Epic Poetry (1727), "Sir Isaac Newton walking in his gardens, had the first thought of his system of gravitation, upon seeing an apple falling from a tree."
evidence.origin: Wikipedia Isaac Newton; underlying biographical scholarship
